title: Thresholdless dynamical instability in transverse $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric scattering systems: The hidden role of bound states in the continuum
abstract: The stationary scattering properties of transverse parity-time ($\mathcal{PT}$) symmetric systems have been extensively studied, yet their dynamical stability, a prerequisite for any stationary description, remains largely unexplored. Here we uncover a thresholdless dynamical instability in such systems, driven by symmetry-protected bound states in the continuum (BICs). Without gain and loss, the up-down mirror symmetry of the transverse geometry generically protects a BIC, which manifests as the coalescence of an $S$-matrix pole and zero on the real axis of the complex wave-number plane. A Hermitian symmetry-breaking perturbation shifts the poles into the lower half-plane, converting the BIC into a resonance with a Fermi-golden-rule decay width. An anti-Hermitian $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric perturbation instead reverses the sign of the second-order energy shift, driving the poles into the upper half-plane and producing a time-growing bound state with $\operatorname{Im}E=γ^{2}Γ_{V}/2+O(γ^{3})$, where $γ$ is the gain-loss strength and $Γ_{V}$ is the golden-rule coupling of the BIC to the continuum. The instability therefore sets in at arbitrarily small $γ$ whenever $Γ_{V}>0$. We confirm this mechanism in a three-site side-coupled model that is unstable despite possessing a unitary scattering matrix, and in a four-site rhombic model where transverse and longitudinal gain-loss placements yield vanishing and finite thresholds, respectively. These results establish a microscopic stability criterion and a design principle for stable $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric scattering devices.
summary: This paper reveals a thresholdless dynamical instability in transverse PT-symmetric scattering systems, showing that the presence of a BIC coupled to the continuum leads to exponential energy growth under anti-Hermitian perturbations. The instability is governed by the spatial overlap between the gain/loss potential and the BIC state, providing a crucial design principle for stable non-Hermitian devices.
main_problem: The paper investigates the dynamical stability of transverse parity-time (PT)-symmetric scattering systems, addressing the gap in knowledge regarding their dynamic stability despite extensive study of their stationary properties.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that an anti-Hermitian PT-symmetric perturbation can drive the system into a time-growing bound state (TGBS) for arbitrarily small gain-loss strength, establishing a microscopic instability criterion.
method: The analysis relies on tracking the poles of the S-matrix in the complex wave-number plane, using perturbation theory (Feshbach projection) to analyze the shift of Bound States in the Continuum (BICs).
model_or_system: The study uses transverse PT-symmetric scattering systems, modeled via tight-binding approaches, specifically examining three-site side-coupled and four-site rhombic models with engineered gain/loss potentials.
key_observables: Pole trajectories in the complex k-plane, the imaginary part of the energy ($	ext{Im } E$), and the time evolution of a localized wave packet showing exponential growth.
important_parameters: Gain-loss strength ($\gamma$), the golden-rule coupling ($\Gamma_V$), and the nature of the perturbation (Hermitian vs. anti-Hermitian).
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes the existence of a single, non-degenerate BIC for simplicity, and the instability mechanism is linked to the spatial overlap between the gain-loss potential and the BIC wave function.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the pole coalescence (BIC), the shift of poles under Hermitian perturbation (lower half-plane), and the upward shift into the first quadrant under PT-symmetric perturbation, accompanied by time evolution plots showing exponential growth.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by noting the gap in dynamical stability studies. It then analyzes the effect of perturbations on the BIC pole structure, contrasting Hermitian and anti-Hermitian cases. Finally, it confirms the instability mechanism using specific lattice models (three-site and four-site rhombic) and derives a design principle.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and open quantum systems as it provides a rigorous stability criterion for engineered non-Hermitian systems, directly impacting the design of stable quantum optical devices.
